title: The Last Leaf
text:
Two young women artists, Sue and Johnsy, shared a studio in a shabby corner of Greenwich Village. In November pneumonia swept the neighborhood, and Johnsy fell gravely ill. The doctor told Sue that her friend had perhaps one chance in ten, and that chance depended on whether she wanted to live.

Johnsy lay staring out of the window at an old ivy vine on the brick wall opposite, counting its leaves as the wind tore them off. When the last one fell, she told Sue, she would die too.

Downstairs lived Behrman, an old painter who had failed at art for forty years, drank too much, and was always going to paint his masterpiece. Sue told him about Johnsy's fancy. He scoffed at it, but he was upset. That night a cold rain and a howling wind beat against the house.

In the morning Johnsy asked Sue to raise the shade. One ivy leaf still clung to the vine. It was there all that day, and through another stormy night. Johnsy grew ashamed of wanting to die, asked for soup, and began to recover.

Then Sue told her the news. Behrman had died of pneumonia after only two days of illness. On the morning of the storm he had been found soaked through, with a lantern, a ladder, brushes and green and yellow paint. On the night the last leaf fell, he had painted it on the wall. It was his masterpiece.
lesson: A quiet act of care for a neighbor can give someone the strength to keep going. The greatest work of your life may be something done for one person.
location: Greenwich Village, New York City, USA
source: O. Henry, The Last Leaf, in The Trimmed Lamp (1907)
